column1: construction-change-order-unapproved-tax-revenue|An unsigned change order does not automatically disappear from a percentage-of-completion calculation. Contract price must reflect the applicable rules for disputed amounts, enforceable rights and reasonably expected receipts. Billing status and tax contract revenue are different questions. An exempt contract using another permissible method needs a separate timing analysis.|A mechanical contractor performs extra ventilation work requested on site. The customer accepts the installation but disputes the additional price. Excluding every disputed dollar could understate estimated contract revenue.|Identify the contract's tax method;Read the change-order and dispute provisions;Document the support for expected collection and update the estimate consistently|Original agreement and amendments;Correspondence acknowledging extra work;Cost and collection forecasts|Do not substitute an accounts-receivable aging report for the contract-price analysis.|An approved price, an unresolved scope claim and an amount the customer has rejected entirely can produce different estimates. The strength of the legal right matters alongside expected collection.|Record the estimated price used for tax and why that estimate remains reasonable at year-end.

construction-contract-spans-december-small-job|Crossing December can make a construction agreement a long-term contract, but it does not automatically require the percentage-of-completion method. Section 460 contains exceptions, including qualifying home-construction contracts and certain other construction contracts meeting the completion-period and small-business tests. An exception still requires a permissible, consistently applied method.|An electrical business starts a short warehouse project in November and finishes in February. The owner assumes crossing the calendar year requires a new accounting system for every job.|Classify the construction activity;Test the relevant receipts and expected completion requirements;Compare the proposed method with prior returns|Signed scope and expected schedule;Gross-receipts aggregation workpaper;Existing tax-method documentation|Small contract value alone does not establish eligibility for the exception.|Expected completion time at contract inception and the statutory gross-receipts test are separate requirements for the small-contractor exception. Related entities can affect the receipts calculation.|Determine eligibility before choosing the method, then document any accounting-method change procedure needed.

contractor-buys-materials-for-next-year-job|Buying materials is not the same as immediately deducting them or earning an equivalent percentage of contract revenue. A percentage-of-completion contractor must identify properly allocable contract costs and apply the applicable allocation rules. A contractor using an exempt method must separately evaluate materials, inventories and its established tax method.|A builder prepays for steel in December while fabrication and installation begin in March. The steel remains at the supplier, and the builder wants the entire payment to reduce current taxable profit.|Confirm title and delivery terms;Tie the materials to the specific contract;Apply the established cost-allocation and recognition method|Purchase order and storage agreement;Supplier invoice and payment evidence;Job-cost ledger|A December bank withdrawal does not settle the tax treatment of materials.|A payment securing future supply differs from owned materials properly allocable to an existing contract. Whether the taxpayer has acquired the property changes the starting analysis.|Reconcile cash paid to materials acquired and tax costs recognized, with no duplicate deduction when used.

contract-cost-overrun-completion-percentage|Under percentage-of-completion reporting, revised estimated total costs generally affect the current cumulative calculation. A later estimate does not automatically mean prior returns were erroneous. A genuine estimate revision differs from an error or a change in accounting method, and completed contracts may require a separate look-back review.|A contractor previously estimated total costs at $800,000. Unexpected site conditions raise the forecast to $1 million. Reusing the old denominator would overstate the current completion percentage.|Reforecast all remaining work;Separate newly learned facts from prior mistakes;Reconcile cumulative income less amounts already reported|Dated estimate versions;Site-condition reports;Prior-year contract schedules|Do not quietly rewrite historical estimates to make the current schedule appear consistent.|Information reasonably unavailable when the earlier return was prepared supports an estimate revision. Ignored invoices or an arithmetic mistake require a different correction analysis.|Preserve the estimate history and explain the current-year catch-up instead of changing past schedules without a basis.

contractor-replaces-subcontractor-unfinished-job|Replacement subcontractor costs can enter the unfinished contract's properly allocable cost pool, but the analysis must also address recoveries and remaining completion costs. A loss-making project does not automatically create a separate immediate deduction for every replacement payment. The contract's tax method continues to govern recognition.|A roofing subcontractor abandons a project. The general contractor hires a replacement at a higher price and pursues the original firm's performance bond. The job forecast now contains both additional costs and a possible recovery.|Identify the work each payment covers;Update estimated total contract costs;Analyze the bond claim without netting unsupported estimates|Subcontracts and replacement bids;Bond correspondence;Revised project budget|Do not count the abandoned subcontractor's unpaid scope and the replacement scope twice in estimated remaining costs.|A bond recovery that is enforceable and reasonably expected differs from a speculative lawsuit. The recovery's treatment must be coordinated with the contract-price and cost rules.|Create one reconciled job forecast showing incurred costs, unfinished scope and separately supported recoveries.

construction-contract-land-separate-activity|A land transfer and construction services bundled in one agreement do not automatically share one tax accounting method. The long-term contract regulations distinguish activities subject to Section 460 from non-long-term-contract activities. Allocation and contract-severing rules can matter even when the customer signs only one document.|A developer agrees to sell a parcel and build a warehouse for a combined price. Treating the entire amount as construction revenue may obscure a separately taxable land transaction.|Identify what property and services transfer;Review the regulatory allocation and severing rules;Support the allocation using the actual economics|Purchase and construction agreement;Land basis and valuation evidence;Closing and project schedules|One invoice does not establish one indivisible activity for federal tax accounting.|A customer buying an existing parcel plus construction services may present different facts from a qualifying home-construction arrangement. Ownership, contract rights and project classification determine the analysis.|Document the land and construction components before calculating contract revenue and recoverable costs.

construction-project-finished-dispute-final-punchlist|A tax completion date is not necessarily the final invoice date or the date the last small defect is corrected. The long-term contract regulations provide completion tests tied to use, incurred allocable costs and final completion and acceptance. Substantial remaining work must be distinguished from routine closeout activity.|A customer begins operating in a completed facility in December. Minor paint and trim work continues in January. The contractor cannot choose the later year solely because a punch list remains open.|Identify when the customer could use the subject matter;Apply the regulatory completion tests;Separate disputed acceptance from minor corrective work|Occupancy and acceptance records;Punch-list detail and costs;Contract closeout correspondence|Do not use the release of retainage as the sole completion test.|Remaining work that materially prevents intended use differs from inexpensive finishing tasks after operational use. Both the nature and amount of unfinished work matter.|Support the tax completion date with project facts, then coordinate final revenue and any look-back obligations.

construction-cancelled-contract-materials-reused|Canceling a construction job does not make reusable materials worthless. Costs must be traced among the terminated contract, recoverable customer claims and materials retained for another job or inventory. A full write-off followed by another deduction when the materials are used would duplicate the same economic cost.|A contractor's customer cancels a retail buildout. Standard fixtures move to a later project while custom signage cannot be reused. The two categories need different recovery analyses.|Inventory what remains after termination;Assign basis to reused or recoverable items;Review termination receipts and the governing contract method|Termination agreement;Material transfer tickets;Salvage and claim documentation|Do not write off the entire job ledger without removing assets still owned and useful.|Reusable stock with continuing value differs from contract-specific materials that cannot be sold or redeployed. Evidence of actual disposition supports the distinction.|Close the canceled job with a cost bridge showing what was recovered, transferred, abandoned or still held.

construction-lookback-customer-final-cost-adjustment|A later final-cost adjustment can require a look-back interest review for a contract reported under percentage of completion. Look-back is not simply a revision of taxable income on old returns: it generally measures the effect of recomputing prior allocations using actual results. Statutory exceptions and de minimis rules must be checked.|A completed commercial project receives a late subcontractor settlement that changes final costs. The owner assumes the current deduction is the only remaining tax step.|Identify the original contract method;Check whether look-back and an exception apply;Determine the redetermination year and required calculation|Original annual contract schedules;Final cost reconciliation;Prior look-back filings|Do not assume a small accounting adjustment is automatically exempt from look-back.|A contract outside mandatory percentage-of-completion rules may be treated differently from one subject to them. The applicable exception must be established rather than inferred from project size.|Document whether Form 8697 or another follow-up is required and retain the supporting exemption calculation if not.

construction-contracts-combine-one-customer|Separate signatures do not guarantee separate contracts for Section 460. Regulations permit or require aggregation or severing when needed to clearly reflect income, considering pricing, negotiations, delivery and the parties' rights. Separate contract accounting must follow the economic arrangement rather than a preferred tax result.|A contractor signs separate foundation and shell agreements with one customer. Both prices were negotiated together, and neither phase would have been undertaken independently.|Compare negotiation and pricing history;Review interdependent performance and acceptance terms;Apply the regulatory aggregation and severing factors|All related agreements;Bid and negotiation records;Phase-level job-cost schedules|Splitting a project into invoices does not by itself create independently reportable contracts.|Independently priced jobs with separate acceptance can differ from interdependent phases sold as one package. Common customer ownership alone does not answer the question.|Write down why the selected unit of account reflects the actual transaction before calculating completion percentages.

manufacturer-small-business-unicap-growth|The small-business exception to Section 263A depends on the applicable gross-receipts test and tax-shelter restrictions, not simply current sales or employee count. Receipts of related businesses may need aggregation. Growing out of the exception can create an accounting-method issue as well as a different year-end inventory calculation.|A manufacturer adds a commonly controlled distribution company and sees combined receipts rise. Looking only at the factory's standalone revenue may give the wrong eligibility answer.|Calculate the prescribed multi-year receipts test;Review aggregation and tax-shelter status;Assess method-change procedures if eligibility changes|Entity ownership chart;Historical receipts by entity;Prior inventory-method elections|Do not reuse a prior-year dollar threshold without checking the relevant year.|A business below the receipts limit can still fail the exception if it is a tax shelter. Ownership and loss allocations therefore matter alongside sales.|Prepare an annual eligibility workpaper before deciding which production costs may be expensed.

factory-idle-capacity-overhead-inventory|An idle factory does not automatically make every production overhead item currently deductible. Section 263A allocation rules address mixed service costs, capacity and certain excluded costs. The manufacturer must distinguish genuine idle-facility costs from production-related overhead allocable to goods actually produced, using a reasonable permitted method.|A factory operates one production line while another is shut down. The owner wants to expense the building's entire rent even though the operating line still uses the space.|Separate facility-wide and line-specific costs;Identify the permitted allocation method;Review whether claimed idle costs meet the regulatory treatment|Capacity and downtime logs;Overhead accounts;Cost-allocation policy|A lower production volume is not evidence that all fixed overhead ceased supporting production.|An identifiable idle facility differs from temporarily reduced output in a facility still producing goods. The actual use of space and services changes the allocation.|Retain a reconciliation between total overhead, excluded amounts and amounts assigned to ending inventory.

manufacturer-offsite-warehouse-capitalization|Moving finished goods offsite does not alone turn storage into a selling expense. Inventory capitalization rules can include storage and handling costs, subject to the applicable exceptions and allocation rules. Whether the business is exempt from Section 263A must be established before applying the more detailed rules.|A furniture maker leases a warehouse for finished products awaiting customer orders. The accountant books the rent to distribution expense, but that label does not settle its tax treatment.|Confirm the business's capitalization requirements;Identify storage versus sales activities;Allocate shared occupancy and handling costs consistently|Warehouse lease;Inventory movement reports;Space and labor allocation records|Do not classify the entire warehouse as a sales office because customers occasionally collect orders there.|Storage before sale differs from a facility used solely for selling activity. Mixed use calls for a supported allocation rather than an all-or-nothing label.|Reconcile warehouse expenses to the tax inventory schedule and document any exception relied upon.

manufacturer-owner-management-time-inventory|Owner compensation can include production-related costs that belong in inventory or produced property. The answer depends on the owner's actual duties, applicable capitalization rules and reasonable allocation. Compensation for selling activities does not become a production cost merely because the same person also supervises the factory.|A salaried owner spends mornings scheduling production and afternoons meeting customers. Expensing the entire salary may omit production management from the cost pool; capitalizing all of it may overstate inventory.|Map actual duties to cost categories;Support a reasonable time or activity allocation;Apply the established tax cost method|Role and time evidence;Payroll reports;Production and sales activity logs|Ownership percentage is not an allocation key for the work performed.|Production supervision, overall administration and direct selling can have different treatment. The actual service performed matters more than the executive title.|Document a practical allocation that follows duties and update it when the owner's role changes.

production-scrap-sale-proceeds-cost-accounting|Scrap receipts must be accounted for consistently with the manufacturer's inventory and income methods. Depending on the facts and permitted method, recoverable scrap value may affect production costs or be separately reported. Either way, the same proceeds cannot both reduce inventory cost and disappear from taxable receipts.|A machine shop sells metal offcuts monthly. The bookkeeper credits materials expense while another system separately records the same checks as revenue, distorting margins and taxable profit.|Trace scrap proceeds to the general ledger;Review the established costing method;Reconcile scrap quantities with production records|Scrap dealer settlements;Material usage reports;Inventory costing policy|Do not adopt a different treatment each year based on which result lowers income.|Routine byproduct recovery differs from selling previously capitalized equipment or inventory. Identify what was actually sold before choosing the account.|Use one documented treatment and reconcile it to both inventory valuation and reported receipts.

factory-rework-costs-unsold-products|Reworking products generally requires the same capitalization analysis as producing them. Direct labor, materials and allocable overhead used to bring unsold goods into saleable condition may remain in inventory instead of becoming an immediate deduction. Abnormal spoilage and worthless goods require separate factual review.|A manufacturer fixes a defective batch in December and ships it in February. Payroll expense on the books does not necessarily mean all repair labor is deductible before the goods are sold.|Identify goods still on hand;Trace repair labor and materials;Distinguish rework from demonstrably worthless or abnormal production losses|Batch quality reports;Rework tickets;Year-end inventory listings|Do not deduct the same rework as both current repair expense and cost of goods sold later.|Successful rework that creates saleable inventory differs from scrapping goods with no remaining value. Evidence of outcome and disposition changes the cost recovery.|Reconcile the reworked batch's total basis and when that basis is recovered through sales or loss treatment.

manufacturer-allocates-interest-production-assets|Interest incurred during production may require capitalization under Section 263A(f), even when it is recorded as ordinary financing expense. The rules depend on the property produced, production period, thresholds and applicable exceptions. A loan's description alone does not establish the tax deduction.|A company borrows for a long fabrication project while also carrying working-capital debt. It cannot assume that only interest on the loan labeled construction is relevant to the capitalization computation.|Classify the produced property;Determine the production period and exception eligibility;Calculate capitalizable interest using the required method|Debt schedules and rates;Production expenditures by date;Placed-in-service records|Do not equate bank interest expense with the current tax deduction without a capitalization review.|Property subject to the interest capitalization rules differs from property outside them. The production characteristics and statutory exceptions determine whether the computation is needed.|Retain a bridge from total interest to capitalized basis, deductible interest and any separate limitation.

manufacturer-self-build-machinery-own-use|Building machinery for internal use normally creates an asset rather than an immediate payroll deduction for every employee hour. Direct wages, materials and appropriate indirect costs must be evaluated for capitalization. Depreciation generally begins when the machine is ready and available for its assigned business use, not when fabrication starts.|Factory technicians spend three months constructing a custom assembly machine. Their pay remains wages for payroll purposes, but its income-tax cost recovery may follow the machine's basis.|Open a separate internal-project cost code;Allocate direct and applicable indirect costs;Document completion and readiness for use|Employee project records;Parts invoices;Testing and commissioning reports|Payroll reporting and income-tax capitalization answer different questions.|Maintenance on an existing machine differs from producing a separate new asset. Define the project and property before deciding the recovery method.|Record the completed machine's supported tax basis and placed-in-service date without duplicating the capitalized wages as expenses.

inventory-tax-method-vs-financial-cost-standard|Standard costs can be useful, but tax inventory must reflect a permissible method that reasonably approximates actual costs and handles variances properly. Unreconciled management standards are not automatically acceptable tax values. Favorable and unfavorable variances need consistent treatment rather than selective year-end adjustments.|A manufacturer holds last year's standard material prices constant while input costs rise. Expensing every unfavorable variance may leave ending inventory below its properly allocable tax cost.|Identify the actual tax inventory method;Analyze material labor and overhead variances;Allocate required variances between sold and unsold goods|Standard cost updates;Actual purchase and production data;Variance reconciliation|Do not use financial reporting convenience as proof that the tax method clearly reflects income.|Minor regularly reviewed variances differ from large stale standards that systematically misstate inventory. Their size and causes affect the correction needed.|Reconcile the standard-cost ledger to a defensible tax inventory amount and review method-change requirements before switching approaches.

manufacturer-outsourced-production-tax-producer|A business can be treated as producing property even when another company performs physical fabrication. Ownership and the benefits and burdens of the production arrangement matter under Section 263A. Outsourcing labor is therefore not enough to conclude that only reseller rules or no production capitalization applies.|A brand supplies raw materials and tooling to a contract factory and bears loss on defective units. It calls itself a distributor because it has no manufacturing employees.|Read ownership and risk provisions;Identify production-related expenditures the business incurs;Apply producer classification and exception rules|Manufacturing agreement;Material ownership records;Reject and insurance policies|Do not classify the business solely by its industry code or employee job titles.|Buying completed goods from an independent vendor differs from arranging production while retaining ownership and production risk. The contract and actual conduct control.|Document the producer-versus-reseller conclusion before selecting which costs enter inventory.

partner-retirement-contribution-guaranteed-payments|A partnership distribution is not the measure of a working partner's retirement-plan compensation. Self-employed earned income requires a calculation using relevant partnership income and adjustments, including the applicable self-employment-tax deduction and plan contribution calculation. Guaranteed payments for services may enter that computation; capital-related receipts require a separate analysis.|A partner receives $90,000 in cash but much less allocable earned income after expenses. Using the cash withdrawal as plan compensation could produce an excessive contribution.|Identify service and capital income separately;Calculate self-employment earnings and required adjustments;Apply the specific plan's contribution formula|Schedule K-1 and supporting schedules;Guaranteed-payment detail;Plan document and contribution workpaper|A large distribution can represent prior earnings or borrowed cash rather than current retirement compensation.|A guaranteed payment for services differs from a payment for use of capital. The nature of the payment can change the earned-income calculation.|Have the contribution calculation reconciled to the partner's return before funding the maximum assumed amount.

partnership-profits-interest-vesting-services|A partnership profits interest is not corporate stock, and vesting does not by itself determine taxability. IRS profits-interest guidance provides conditions under which receipt and vesting can avoid a taxable event. The parties' treatment as partners, the absence of a compensation deduction and the nature of the interest are central.|An LLC taxed as a partnership awards a manager future upside subject to continued service. The documents must distinguish future profits from a share of existing liquidation value.|Determine the entity's tax classification;Test the award against the profits-interest guidance;Coordinate partner reporting from the grant date where required|Grant and operating agreements;Liquidation-value analysis;Vesting schedule and K-1 treatment|Do not copy a corporate option template and assume it establishes a partnership safe harbor.|An interest worth something in a hypothetical immediate liquidation can be a capital interest. That changes the starting tax analysis even if the agreement calls it profits-only.|Document the award's economics and whether Revenue Procedure 2001-43 conditions are satisfied before deciding what elections or filings are needed.

partner-capital-interest-for-services-value|A partnership capital interest received for services can create taxable compensation based on its value, subject to the applicable vesting and Section 83 rules. The profits-interest guidance does not automatically protect an award of existing equity value. The partnership must coordinate the recipient's income with its own deduction or capitalization treatment.|An established consulting LLC gives a new manager a share of current assets and retained value without a cash contribution. Calling the award sweat equity does not make that current value tax-free.|Determine immediate liquidation rights;Establish value and restrictions;Coordinate the recipient's inclusion and partnership reporting|Updated operating agreement;Valuation and capital accounts;Service and vesting terms|A zero cash purchase price does not establish zero fair market value.|An award limited to future appreciation differs from one sharing value already accumulated. Liquidation economics expose that distinction more reliably than the award's label.|Resolve valuation and timing before issuing the K-1 or claiming a compensation deduction.

partner-health-insurance-paid-guaranteed-payment|Partners generally are not employees of the partnership for federal employment-tax purposes. Health premiums paid on a partner's behalf commonly require guaranteed-payment and partner-income reporting rather than ordinary employee exclusion treatment. A separate self-employed health-insurance deduction may be available subject to its own requirements and limitations.|A partnership pays the same insurer for two employees and one working partner. The employee benefit entries cannot simply be copied into the partner's tax reporting.|Identify whose coverage was purchased;Determine guaranteed-payment and K-1 treatment;Review the partner-level deduction and other coverage eligibility|Premium statements by insured;Partnership payment records;K-1 and partner deduction workpapers|Do not omit partner income merely because the partnership paid the insurer directly.|Eligibility for subsidized coverage through another employer can affect the partner's deduction. It does not turn the partner into a common-law employee of this partnership.|Reconcile the partnership deduction, partner inclusion and any personal deduction so the premiums are neither omitted nor deducted twice.

llc-partner-receives-w2-through-disregarded-entity|A partnership generally cannot convert a partner into an employee by routing pay through its wholly owned disregarded entity. Although a disregarded entity can have separate employment-tax responsibilities for employees, the partner rule still applies to partners of its owner. Actual tax classification must be checked.|A two-member partnership owns a single-member operating LLC. One partner wants the operating LLC to issue a W-2 so the compensation resembles everyone else's payroll.|Confirm both entities' tax classifications;Identify the individual's ownership relationship;Correct compensation and benefits reporting consistently|Ownership chart and elections;Payroll history;Operating agreements|A separate EIN does not necessarily create a separate employer relationship for this partner.|An entity taxed as a corporation can present a different compensation framework. A disregarded LLC is not the same arrangement merely because it has its own bank account.|Coordinate payroll corrections with guaranteed payments, self-employment tax and benefit-plan reporting before changing the payment channel.

partnership-representative-binds-owners-consent|Under the centralized partnership audit regime, a properly designated partnership representative generally has broad authority to act for the partnership, and partners can be bound by those actions. Internal approval limits in an operating agreement do not necessarily restrict that authority before the IRS. Contractual remedies among owners are a separate issue.|An agreement requires unanimous approval before settling an audit, but the designated representative accepts an IRS adjustment. The owners cannot assume their internal voting provision makes the settlement ineffective.|Confirm whether the centralized regime applies;Identify the valid representative and designated individual;Coordinate IRS authority with internal notice and approval procedures|Filed representative designation;Operating agreement;Audit correspondence and settlement records|Do not confuse an internal breach of contract with a limit on the representative's statutory authority.|An eligible partnership that validly elects out follows a different audit framework. Determine the applicable regime before assuming individual partner consent controls.|Choose the representative deliberately and establish communications and contractual protections before an audit begins.

partnership-tax-distribution-exceeds-profit-share|A tax distribution is generally a distribution to an owner, not a partnership income-tax deduction. A payment above current allocated profit can reduce outside basis and, when money exceeds available basis, potentially trigger gain. Liability changes and other basis adjustments must be considered before reaching that conclusion.|A partnership uses a high assumed tax rate to fund an owner's estimated taxes. The resulting cash payment exceeds that owner's current profit allocation, but that alone does not tell whether gain arises.|Reconcile the distribution to the agreement;Update outside basis including liability changes;Test the cash distribution against available basis|Distribution ledger;Outside-basis rollforward;Debt allocation schedules|A bookkeeping label of tax reimbursement does not create a deductible operating expense.|An owner can have basis from earlier contributions or debt even in a low-profit year. Current profit alone is therefore not the distribution's tax ceiling.|Prepare a partner-level basis calculation and distinguish distribution policy from deductible compensation.

partnership-audit-optout-disregarded-entity-partner|Having fewer than 100 partners does not by itself establish eligibility to elect out of the centralized partnership audit regime. Partner types and the counting rules matter. A disregarded entity partner generally prevents the election under the applicable eligibility rules, even when its owner would otherwise be an eligible individual.|A ten-owner partnership admits one owner through a single-member disregarded LLC. The preparer cannot assume the small headcount preserves the annual opt-out election.|Identify every direct partner's tax classification;Apply eligible-partner and counting rules;Review the annual election and notification requirements|Partner ownership and classification records;Filed Schedule B-2;Partner notification evidence|Do not look through a disregarded LLC solely to substitute its individual owner for the eligibility test.|A direct individual partner differs from a disregarded entity holding the interest. Some S-corporation shareholders also affect the partner count, so headcount alone is insufficient.|Assess eligibility before filing the election and review proposed ownership changes with the partnership preparer.

joint-equipment-use-partnership-tax-exclusion|Separate customer invoices do not by themselves establish that a joint arrangement is outside partnership tax reporting. First determine whether the activity creates a partnership for federal tax purposes. Some qualifying arrangements can elect exclusion from parts of Subchapter K under Section 761, but eligibility and election requirements are narrow and factual.|Two businesses jointly own and use specialized equipment while each serves its own customers. Pooling operating profits and selling services together could change the arrangement even if the customer invoices remain separate.|Identify ownership activity and profit-sharing rights;Distinguish mere coownership from a joint business;Test any Section 761 exclusion and election requirements|Equipment ownership agreement;Operating and customer contracts;Separate income and cost records|Do not assume separate bank accounts or invoices eliminate a jointly conducted business.|Qualifying joint use of property differs from an organization jointly selling services or output. Each participant's ability to compute income independently is also relevant under the exclusion rules.|Have the arrangement classified before omitting Form 1065 and document the specific exclusion and procedural basis if one applies.

partner-guaranteed-payment-due-unpaid-yearend|An unpaid guaranteed payment needs coordinated timing analysis under the partnership rules, accounting methods and any applicable related-party provisions. The date cash changes hands is not the only relevant fact, and a guaranteed payment cannot be treated as an ordinary draw to avoid recipient income. Deductibility also depends on whether the payment must be capitalized.|A partnership accrues a fixed annual management payment in December but pays it in February. The preparer must reconcile the partnership's tax year with the partner's reporting year rather than assuming a simple cash-basis mismatch.|Confirm the obligation is a guaranteed payment;Review tax-year and accounting-method rules;Determine deduction or capitalization and partner inclusion together|Operating agreement and accrual;Payment date evidence;Both parties' tax-year information|Do not deduct the accrual while ignoring the corresponding partner reporting rule.|A fixed service payment differs from an amount dependent on partnership income. Classification must be established before deciding timing.|Create one timing workpaper explaining the partnership's treatment and the year reported to the partner.

corporate-redemption-spouse-retains-shares|A complete redemption of shares directly held by an owner does not automatically qualify as a sale when family attribution applies. Stock owned by a spouse can be treated as owned by the redeemed shareholder. Section 302 tests, possible attribution waivers and continuing relationships require careful review.|A corporation redeems all of one spouse's shares while the other remains the controlling shareholder. The redeemed spouse expects capital-gain treatment simply because the personal stock certificate is canceled.|Map direct and attributed ownership;Test the Section 302 alternatives;Review waiver conditions before relying on complete termination|Ownership before and after redemption;Redemption agreement;Family and continuing-interest facts|Zero directly owned shares does not necessarily mean zero ownership for the redemption tests.|A valid family-attribution waiver has conditions beyond transferring shares. Continued interests and prohibited reacquisitions can affect eligibility.|Determine sale-versus-distribution treatment before calculating stock basis recovery or estimating the seller's tax.

corporation-buys-treasury-stock-deduction|A corporation generally cannot deduct the purchase price of its own shares as an operating expense. The transaction changes capital ownership rather than purchasing deductible services. Stock-repurchase costs also have specific restrictions, and any separate interest, compensation or excise-tax issue requires its own analysis.|A corporation pays a departing shareholder $250,000 and books it as an owner separation expense. That account name does not make the redemption price deductible.|Separate share price from other obligations;Review transaction-cost restrictions;Coordinate corporate entries with shareholder redemption treatment|Repurchase agreement;Closing statement;Board authorization and fee invoices|Do not treat a redemption as payroll merely because the shareholder previously worked for the company.|A genuine separately substantiated service payment differs from consideration for shares. Substance and negotiated terms must support the distinction.|Classify each component before filing and remove the share purchase price from ordinary business deductions.

founder-contributes-property-corp-liabilities|A property contribution can qualify for nonrecognition under Section 351 only when its requirements are met. Debt assumption introduces additional rules, including potential gain when liabilities exceed adjusted basis and exceptions for certain deductible liabilities. Control, transfer purpose and the actual property basis all matter.|A founder transfers appreciated equipment and its loan to a new corporation. The loan exceeds the equipment's adjusted tax basis, even though the corporation receives positive market equity.|Test Section 351 control and property requirements;Compare assumed liabilities with tax basis;Calculate corporate and shareholder bases after any recognized gain|Asset basis and depreciation records;Loan documents;Formation and stock issuance records|Positive fair market equity does not eliminate a liabilities-over-basis problem.|Tax basis differs from appraised value. A debt-covered asset can create gain even when its market value comfortably exceeds the loan.|Complete the liability and basis computation before treating the formation as entirely tax-free.

c-corp-dividend-book-retained-earnings-ep|Book retained earnings and tax earnings and profits are different measures. A C-corporation distribution can be a dividend despite zero book retained earnings if current or accumulated tax E&P supports dividend treatment. Only after the applicable E&P analysis can stock basis recovery and potential gain be determined.|A corporation reports an accounting loss after book depreciation but has different tax adjustments. The owner cannot infer return-of-capital treatment from the balance sheet alone.|Calculate current and accumulated tax E&P;Identify all distributions and their dates;Apply the ordering and allocation rules|Historical returns;Book-to-tax and E&P schedules;Distribution ledger and stock basis|Do not use a negative retained-earnings account as a substitute for an E&P study.|Book expenses and tax depreciation adjustments can move E&P differently from accounting income. The historical tax computation changes the classification.|Support the dividend portion before preparing shareholder reporting or reducing stock basis.

redeemable-preferred-stock-book-liability-tax|Financial-statement liability classification does not automatically make preferred-stock payments deductible interest for federal tax. Debt-versus-equity treatment requires analysis of the instrument's legal rights and economic substance. Tax rules for particular preferred instruments can also affect distributions and transactions without converting every payment into interest.|A corporation issues redeemable preferred shares and its accountant presents them as a liability. The owner wants to deduct the scheduled preferred return as loan interest.|Read the full instrument and redemption terms;Analyze federal debt-equity factors;Coordinate payment classification and information reporting|Share terms and offering documents;Payment schedules;Book classification memo and tax analysis|A GAAP balance-sheet label does not resolve federal tax character.|An enforceable creditor relationship differs from an equity investment carrying preferred economic rights. Subordination, participation and repayment terms help establish the distinction.|Obtain a supported instrument classification before taking interest deductions or treating payments as dividends.

company-capital-contribution-employee-stock-right|Cash invested in a corporation and shares awarded for services are separate tax events. A cash contribution may increase stock basis, while compensatory shares can create income under Section 83 based on value and restrictions. Combining the transactions in one board resolution does not erase the service component.|A founder invests $50,000 and receives additional equity for a year of unpaid management work. The full share issuance cannot automatically be treated as purchased solely with the cash.|Allocate shares to cash and services;Value the compensatory interest;Review vesting timing and any relevant election deadline|Subscription and service agreements;Board resolutions;Valuation and payroll records|Do not treat unpaid labor as tax basis equal to an invented hourly charge.|Shares acquired at fair value for cash differ from value transferred as compensation. Restricted shares introduce additional timing questions.|Document the consideration for each issuance and coordinate corporate compensation reporting with the founder's stock basis.

corporate-liquidation-shareholder-basis-zero|A complete C-corporation liquidation generally treats shareholder distributions as payment in exchange for stock. Zero stock basis can therefore mean the liquidation amount produces shareholder gain rather than tax-free recovery. Corporate-level gain on distributed or sold assets must be evaluated separately.|An owner previously recovered all stock basis and later receives cash when the corporation liquidates. The existence of a final corporate return does not absorb the shareholder-level tax.|Confirm a complete liquidation plan;Calculate money and property received;Coordinate shareholder gain with corporate asset treatment|Liquidation plan;Stock basis history;Final asset and distribution schedules|Do not assume that paying corporate tax makes the remaining liquidation proceeds tax-free personally.|Liquidation exchange treatment differs from an ordinary dividend distribution.
